content: The Antigua Charter on Sound Management of Public Health Pesticides was adopted in September 2011 following a regional advisory meeting organized by PAHO/WHO in Guatemala from August 23–25, 2011. This charter emphasizes the importance of providing countries with access to best practices in the registration and life-cycle management of public health pesticides through the development of peer-reviewed, authoritative guidelines. These guidelines, created through international expert consultations, aim to harmonize procedures, criteria, and requirements for pesticide management across countries. The WHO Pesticide Evaluation Scheme (WHOPES) has taken a leading role in developing guidelines for pesticide management, efficacy testing, risk assessment, and training. These include the FAO/WHO Guidelines for the Registration of Pesticides (2010), Guidelines for Quality Control of Pesticides (2011), and Guidelines on Data Requirements for Pesticide Registration (2013). Additionally, WHOPES has developed specific guidelines for public health pesticide management policies tailored to the African and South-East Asia regions, as well as efficacy testing protocols for household insecticides, mosquito repellents, spatial repellents, and long-lasting insecticidal nets. Risk assessment models have also been developed by WHO to evaluate the safety of pesticides used in indoor residual spraying, larviciding, and space spraying. These models are essential for ensuring that pesticides are used safely and effectively without causing harm to human health or the environment. Training tools, such as manuals for pesticide specifications, have been created to support capacity building in pesticide quality control. The FAO/WHO Joint Meeting on Pesticide Specifications (JMPS) has been instrumental in developing international standards for pesticide quality control and trade. However, WHO specifications for technical materials are not automatically applicable to similar products from other manufacturers unless equivalence is established. The International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management urges the pesticide industry to ensure that products entering international trade conform to WHO-recommended specifications. Annual JMPS open meetings with industry stakeholders and the Collaborative International Pesticides Analytical Council (CIPAC) have facilitated dialogue and collaboration on pesticide management. Technical support has been provided to 12 priority countries across five WHO regions to assess pesticide management practices, identify country-specific needs, and develop National Action Plans. This support included evaluating the capacity of pesticide quality control laboratories, training regulatory staff, and addressing deficiencies in infrastructure, equipment, and operational procedures. However, many laboratories focus on agricultural pesticides and lack the capacity to test public health pesticides comprehensively. The WHOPES global network has expanded significantly since 2009, with the addition of new WHO Collaborating Centres and partner institutions. This network supports the testing and evaluation of public health pesticides and serves as a resource for national and regional excellence in pesticide management. The project has highlighted the need for a multisectoral approach to pesticide life-cycle management, involving collaboration between health, agriculture, and environmental sectors. This approach ensures effective legislation and practices to maximize the benefits of pesticide use while minimizing adverse effects on human and animal health and the environment. The establishment of National Steering Committees in participating countries has been a key achievement, promoting collaboration among sectors and optimizing the use of limited resources. The project has also strengthened international collaboration, particularly between WHO and FAO, through joint meetings and the development of harmonized guidance documents. Despite these achievements, challenges remain, particularly in addressing weaknesses in pesticide legislation and national policies. WHO, in collaboration with FAO and UNEP, has initiated revisions to the International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management and developed guidelines on pesticide legislation and national policy. Future investments in public health pesticide management should prioritize the development of comprehensive policies and legislation, integration into national health policies, and the establishment of mechanisms for intersectoral cooperation.
